extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of comparative government / political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and assessing constitutional and institutional features of Swiss cantonal governments (composition, selection methods, powers, and civic practices) as described in historical letters. Focus is on how authority is organized, balanced, and exercised in individual cantons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government / composition of three powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The governments of the cantons show "the most evident traces of a composition of all of the three powers in all of them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly emphasises that cantonal constitutions are neither "simple democracy" nor simple aristocracy/monarchy but mixtures: a monarchical power in a chief magistrate, an aristocratical power in councils, and a democratical power in general assemblies. Used as a criterion to judge whether a polity is truly 'simple' or 'mixed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereignty in the general assembly (male suffrage at 15)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sovereignty resides in the general assembly, where each male of fifteen years of age has admittance and a voice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General assembly commonly ratifies laws, lays taxes, enters alliances, declares war and makes peace. Presence and real power of the general assembly (and who is admitted) is a key indicator of how democratic a canton is. Several cantons (e.g., Glaris, Zug, Uri, Switz) are cited as having such assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief magistrate (land amman) as monarchical element
rubrics_metrics.description: Most cantons have a first magistrate (land amman) who is the chief of the republic and presides over parts of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details include methods of appointment (often a mixture of election and lot), alternating confessional selection (Protestant vs Catholic), and differing term lengths (e.g., Protestant three years, Catholic two). The land amman embodies the monarchical or executive face of the canton and is a focal point for evaluating executive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power vested in a senate / council of regency
rubrics_metrics.description: A council (often called a 'senate' or 'council of regency') is commonly the body in which executive authority resides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 'council of regency' composed of senators (numbers vary by canton) runs ordinary administration and provides executive functions. Evaluators should check composition, selection, and scope of this council versus the general assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (legislative, executive, judicial distinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive and judicial powers are separated from legislative functions; various specialized chambers exist for justice and police (e.g., chambers of seven, fifteen, nine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text highlights separate chambers for justice, finance, and police; existence of courts of justice and distinct administrative bodies. The presence and functioning of separate judicial/administrative chambers is used to assess institutional checks and rule-of-law structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple councils and internal checks (grand, little, weekly councils)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantons employ multiple councils (grand council, little/weekly council, secret chamber, chambers of seven/nine/fifteen) that deliberate at different frequencies and on different matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Appenzel's general sovereign council of 144, grand council of 128, weekly council meeting every week. These layered bodies serve as internal checks, distribute responsibilities (legislation, execution, criminal jurisdiction) and prevent concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection mechanisms (lot, ballot, election) to guard against oligarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of lotteries, ballots, and complex mixed procedures to select officers and fill vacancies (e.g., drawing balls, nomination procedures) to limit family influence and oligarchic capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed procedures given (Berne's gold/silver ball draws; Fribourg's box with partitions; Soleure nomination/confirmation rituals). These mechanisms are presented as deliberate anti-oligarchy safeguards and are a criterion for assessing impartiality and openness of recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivisions and local representation (communities/quarters supply delegates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantons are subdivided into communities, quarters, tagwen/corvees, or genossamen which each furnish councillors/senators and have internal officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation is apportioned by locality (e.g., Appenzel's twelve communities, Zug's five quarters). Evaluators should look at how local subdivisions feed into higher bodies and whether representation is balanced between city and countryside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term lengths and tenure (life offices vs fixed terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offices are for life while others have fixed short terms (e.g., avoyers for life; treasurers for six years; bannerets for four years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tenure regimes indicate stability and aristocratic permanence (life terms) versus rotation and accountability (shorter terms). This affects susceptibility to oligarchy and ability to adapt to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and formal qualifications (citizenship, age thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rules for holding office and for participation are specified (e.g., to be eligible to the grand council must be a citizen and at least thirty; suffrage for assemblies commonly begins at fifteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formal thresholds shape who exercises sovereignty and who may be governed; they are essential for evaluating inclusiveness and democratic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability / suitability for large states
rubrics_metrics.description: Small canton constitutions are often praised for balance but judged "imperfectly digested" and "would never be found capable of holding together a great nation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text treats the capacity of institutional arrangements to scale as a criterion — structures that work in small agrarian polities may fail in large, populous states, particularly where executive strength is insufficient for defense or cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia system and civic obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Every male of fifteen is enrolled in the militia and obliged to provide uniform, musket, powder and ball; arms are inspected annually and local arsenals exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia enrolment is discussed as a social and political institution supporting defence and civic discipline; it also intersects with marriage and social status (must produce arms to marry). Presence and organization of militia reflect civic culture and state capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic base influencing political structure (commerce vs noble leisure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence or absence of commerce/manufacture affects the character of government; cantons where ruling families cannot be merchants preserve oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fribourg's forty families govern while eschewing commerce; lack of merchant class maintains oligarchic dominance. Economic foundations are thus a criterion for assessing the persistence of aristocratic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals process and risk of judicial partiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals lie to central courts but judges on appeal are often persons who have been or expect to be bailiffs, creating risk of partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: Bern where bailiffs are powerful and appellate judges are drawn from the same class. Evaluators should examine appointment pathways and conflict-of-interest risks in appellate systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political training institutions for youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cantons maintain political seminaries ("exterior state") which simulate government offices for youth as a training ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a mechanism to create experienced future administrators: youths form grand council, senate, avoyers, etc., debate political subjects, and learn by exercise. Presence of such training indicates institutionalized elite reproduction and preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of secret councils for sensitive affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist secret councils (secret chamber) composed of senior officers for matters requiring secrecy and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret council membership and functions vary; they debate important and confidential affairs. Their existence signals a tiered decision-making process and is relevant to transparency assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks against popular dominance via aristocratical preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocratical preferences and institutional divisions are deliberately arranged to counterbalance popular assemblies and avoid the concentration of authority in one body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: division into councils, officers appointed by lot, and multiple assemblies are explicitly described as ways to check the general assembly (Appenzel, Underwald). Use this to evaluate how a constitution prevents mob rule or unchecked majorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation of offices between confessional (religious) groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Some offices are rotated between Protestants and Catholics (e.g., the land amman alternately chosen from Protestants and Catholics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confessional balance is institutionalized (term lengths may differ by confession). This is a criterion for assessing religious accommodation and power-sharing mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed oligarchic composition and limited families' participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain cantons have only a small number of families who participate in government (e.g., Fribourg: "not having more than forty families, who can have any part in the government").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to label a canton as aristocratical/oligarchic: very few families monopolize offices, use of formal mechanisms (lots/partitions) notwithstanding. Evaluators should note number of families with access to offices and whether membership is effectively closed.
